Table 1 provides a detailed comparison of the aforemen- tioned processes in terms of their ability to control electro- lyte particle sizes and distributions. In summary, strategies for controlling electrolyte particle size include solid-phase, liquid-phase, and unconventional synthesis methods, each with distinct advantages and challenges. The solid-phase approaches, including high-energy milling, sintering, and sieving, offer simplicity and cost-effectiveness but are often limited by particle heterogeneity, the introduction of impu- rities, and energy inefficiency [113–115]. The liquid-phase methods, such as solubility regulation and solvent polar- ity manipulation, enable precise control over particle size and stoichiometry but are limited by solvent toxicity, com- plex post-processing steps, and high costs [116, 117]. The unconventional techniques such as jet milling, raw material pretreatment, and freeze-drying demonstrate unique poten- tial for refining particle sizes and enhancing electrochemi- cal performance but are constrained by material selectivity, high equipment demands, and poor scalability.
